clue.text: this pathetic specimen spewed out (4)

indicators.note: a specimen is a small sample cut out of something larger, which is exactly what a run of consecutive letters is

blocks.note: four consecutive letters that start in the last letter of one word and finish inside the next

explanation.walkthrough: 'Specimen' does two jobs at once: in the story it is the pathetic creature being sneered at, and in the wordplay it is the instruction to take a sample of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: spewed out -> SPAT: the past tense of spit, ejecting something forcibly from the mouth, which is what spewing something out is.

clue.text: a parcel - after removing wrappings, the girl! A sign in the sky (6)

indicators.note: the wrapping of a parcel is what encloses it, so the letters at each end come off and the middle is kept

blocks.note: PARCEL unwrapped: the P at the front and the EL at the back come away
the pronoun that stands in for a girl already named

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the storyteller's voice rather than a signal, and the sign wanted is Sagittarius — the zodiac, not the weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A sign in the sky -> ARCHER: Sagittarius, the zodiac sign drawn as a bowman, goes by that plain English name.

clue.text: stupendous and uplifting to one of strong beliefs (5)

indicators.note: a piece lifted up in a down entry climbs the grid, so its letters arrive bottom to top

blocks.note: something stupendous is big on a scale that impresses
the two letters of the little word, climbing the column and so read the other way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stupendous and uplifting' reads as praise, which is the last tone the answer deserves; that mismatch between surface and sense is the setter's joke.
explanation.definitionFit: one of strong beliefs -> BIGOT: the kindest possible wording for someone whose opinions are held so rigidly that no argument can shift them.

clue.text: developed there at noon to foreshadow (8)

indicators.note: something developed has been worked up into a new shape, and a new shape for a set of letters is a new order for them

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder, taken straight from the clue
N is the standard abbreviation for noon, as printed on a timetable

explanation.walkthrough: 'Developed' is the shuffle. Anagram THERE AT together with the N of noon and the eight letters fall into THREATEN.
explanation.definitionFit: to foreshadow → THREATEN: when the sky threatens rain it is giving warning of rain to come, so to threaten a thing is to foreshadow it.

clue.text: a well-mannered fellow, extremely ideal, being nobility formerly (10)

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are the letters at its two far ends, and both of them are wanted

blocks.note: a gent is a gentleman, the courteous sort
the first and last letters of ideal, in that order
esse is the Latin 'to be', borrowed into English for a thing's very being

explanation.walkthrough: The word is Chaucer's, which is why the definition has to say 'formerly': the surface's well-mannered fellow is describing the very quality being built.
explanation.definitionFit: nobility formerly -> GENTILESSE: the medieval word for nobility of birth and of conduct together, long obsolete, which is what 'formerly' warns you about.

clue.text: Once upon a time, one of great skill (6)

indicators.note: a piece resting upon another is laid against it, which fixes this chunk at the front of the assembly

blocks.note: an ex is what somebody once was, as in ex-president
'twice a day' and 'twice per day' say the same thing, so the article swaps for the Latin
t is the standard abbreviation for time, as in any physics formula

explanation.walkthrough: This is the puzzle's opening line and the fairy tale's, so 'Once upon a time' looks like scene-setting; not one of its four words is spare.
explanation.definitionFit: one of great skill -> EXPERT: the noun sense, someone whose skill is authoritative enough to be called on for it.

clue.text: a prince, one in a guardian's care having Balls, perhaps above all (6)

indicators.note: the surname named is only one of the people carrying that first name, and 'perhaps' is what marks a definition by example
in a down entry the piece put above everything else takes the top cells, so it is written first

blocks.note: Ed Balls was the Labour MP and shadow chancellor, one of several public figures with that first name
a child placed in a guardian's legal care is that guardian's ward

explanation.walkthrough: The capital B is surface work: it makes 'Balls' look like a dance at the palace instead of a politician's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: a prince -> EDWARD: definition by example, the name of several English kings and of the present Duke of Edinburgh.

clue.text: intoxicated by head royal's title (8)

indicators.note: standing by something means standing next to it, so these two pieces simply run together in the order given

blocks.note: somebody high on a drug is intoxicated by it
a ness is a headland, a promontory running out into the sea — Orford Ness, Sheerness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' wants to mean chief or boss and means a bit of coastline instead; that geographical sense is worth banking, because setters reach for it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: royal's title -> HIGHNESS: the form of address a prince or princess takes, always preceded by Your, His or Her.

clue.text: quietly commandeering, located centrally between two poles in a movable chair (5)

indicators.note: a letter taken centrally is the one standing at the exact midpoint of a word, and three words here give one each
the poles of the earth are north and south, so their initials go one at each end of what they enclose

blocks.note: S for south and N for north, one letter at each end of the build
the middle letter of the word itself, the fourth of its seven
the seventh letter of thirteen, dead centre
the middle letter of another seven-letter word

explanation.walkthrough: The poles of the surface are the chair's own carrying poles; in the wordplay they are the earth's. Note that 'located' is fodder as well as sentence — two middles would leave the entry a letter short.
explanation.definitionFit: a movable chair -> SEDAN: the sedan chair, an enclosed seat slung on poles and carried by two bearers, was the taxi of Georgian towns.

clue.text: Thin and straggly, see the tragic princess upset, supported by the old queen inside! (7)

indicators.note: something upset has been tipped over, so the two letters come back the other way round
in a down entry whatever supports a piece sits underneath it, which puts this chunk second
the assembled chunk is dropped into the middle of another word rather than joined on at either end

blocks.note: to spy something is to see it, and these three letters open up after the second
Diana, who died in the 1997 Paris crash, is DI to crosswords — here turned over
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cypher on British postboxes

explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is the word most likely to be read as a link between two halves of the clue, and it is the outer shell of the whole build.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin and straggly -> SPIDERY: said of handwriting or of legs, thin and sprawling in the way a spider's limbs are.

clue.text: a sorcerer, was (when hidden) longing (5)

indicators.note: what is hidden is put out of sight, so the letters named disappear and only the remainder shows

blocks.note: 'when' can be swapped for 'as' — 'as I arrived' — and hiding AS inside WAS leaves a single letter
an itch for something is a longing for it

explanation.walkthrough: The bracket looks like an aside in the story and is the whole instruction: 'when' is there as a synonym, to name the two letters that go.
explanation.definitionFit: a sorcerer -> WITCH: one who works magic; the word covered either sex in older use, though the fairy tale has fixed it as a woman.

clue.text: for, primarily, the emperor's stepdaughter. The emperor's daughter objected (9)

indicators.note: what comes primarily comes first, so each word gives up only its opening letter — and the instruction carries on past the full stop

blocks.note: to be pro something is to be for it, as in pro-European
the opening letters of these three words, in the order the clue sets them down
the same trick again on the next three words

explanation.walkthrough: The full stop is a genuine sentence break in the story running through this puzzle, and it hides the fact that one instruction governs both halves.
explanation.definitionFit: objected -> PROTESTED: to protest is to voice an objection out loud, and the past tense matches.

clue.text: concerned with needing rest, and left (7)

blocks.note: re means concerning, the word at the head of a memo
somebody who needs a rest is tired

explanation.walkthrough: 'Concerned with' looks like the definition of a whole word and is only two letters; the definition is the single word at the very end, which is the last place anyone looks.
explanation.definitionFit: left -> RETIRED: the sense of withdrawing from a room or a field, so it substitutes straight into 'he left after dinner'.

clue.text: Couple having split, he, initially leaving her for a decisive struggle (3-7)

indicators.note: the letter a word starts with is the one picked out here, and it is the letter that has to go
whatever leaves a word is subtracted from it, so the named letter comes out of the front

blocks.note: to couple two things is to tie them together — a verb, not the pair in the surface
a split between two people is a break
HER loses the H that 'he' begins with

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a marriage coming apart and the answer is out of the sports pages; the switch of 'Couple' from noun to verb is the step that unlocks it.
explanation.definitionFit: a decisive struggle -> TIE-BREAKER: the extra contest played to settle a draw, in tennis or anywhere else a result has to be produced.

clue.text: Hot, horribly lost, occasionally mean (6)

indicators.note: a thing done horribly comes out badly formed, and badly formed letters are letters out of their proper order
what happens occasionally happens every so often rather than all the time, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: four letters of fodder, straight from the clue
the second and fourth letters of mean, taken every other one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' is the whole trick: goods too hot to handle are goods the police are looking for. Read as temperature it hides the definition in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot -> STOLEN: thieves' slang, as in 'hot goods' — property taken so recently that handling it is dangerous.

clue.text: seconds after, succeeded stabbing the flying lover-boy with arrows and teeth! (7)

indicators.note: a piece that comes after the rest is tacked on at the end, whichever order the clue names it in
a blade stabbing something ends up buried inside it, and that is where this letter lands

blocks.note: the winged Roman god of love with his bow; the name opens up after its second letter
s. is the genealogist's abbreviation for succeeded
s is the abbreviation for seconds on any stopwatch

explanation.walkthrough: Two different S abbreviations in one clue, and the exclamation mark belongs to the fairy tale rather than to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: teeth -> CUSPIDS: the pointed canines, named for the single cusp each one carries, so this is teeth of a particular kind.

clue.text: he cursed endlessly, unravelling with no less depravity - (13)

indicators.note: a word without its end has lost its final letter, and only what survives goes into the mix
something unravelling comes apart thread by thread, and the threads are laid down again in a new order

blocks.note: HE CURSED with its last letter gone: seven letters of fodder
the two little words used as themselves, six more letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'With no less' reads as an emphatic aside — depravity, no less — and it is nearly half the fodder. A phrase that sounds like commentary is the best hiding place there is.
explanation.definitionFit: depravity -> LECHEROUSNESS: the noun for habitual lustfulness, one particular form of moral depravity rather than the whole of it.

clue.text: She, left aside with no answer, cracked - wanting the protector of her body (8)

definitions.text: wanting the protector of her body

indicators.note: saying a thing goes without something is the plainest way of removing it, so that letter never joins the mix
something cracked has broken into pieces, and the pieces go back together in a different arrangement

blocks.note: the pronoun used as itself, three letters of fodder
L is the standard abbreviation for left
ASIDE once the A has gone: four more letters for the mix
A is the abbreviation for answer, and it is the letter taken out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Left aside' reads as one idiom and is two separate scraps of fodder, which is why counting the letters before splitting the phrase gets you nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: wanting the protector of her body -> HIDELESS: a hide is an animal's skin, the body's own armour, and the -less suffix takes it away.

clue.text: engaged in combat, tenderly to be present (6)

indicators.note: to be engaged in something is to be busy inside it, so the letters are already sitting within the words that follow

blocks.note: the run begins inside the first word and finishes inside the second, straight across the comma

explanation.walkthrough: The letters cross a comma and a word break, which is exactly where the eye stops looking; punctuation counts for nothing once you are reading letters.
explanation.definitionFit: to be present -> ATTEND: to attend a meeting is to be there in person, the infinitive matching the clue's 'to be'.

clue.text: ego invested in dealing an abusive harangue (6)

indicators.note: money invested in a business goes into it, and so does this letter, landing inside the other word rather than beside it

blocks.note: dealing in goods is trade, and the word splits open after its first letter
the ego is the I, the self as Freud's English translators named it

explanation.walkthrough: Ego = I is a convention worth owning: Freud wrote das Ich, the I, and the crossword has used the single letter for it ever since.
explanation.definitionFit: an abusive harangue -> TIRADE: a plain synonym for a long, angry, unbroken outpouring aimed at somebody.

clue.text: The electric superstar, least surprisingly - (5)

indicators.note: a surprise is something turning up where you did not expect it, and so is every letter of the fodder

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, the whole of the word

explanation.walkthrough: One word of fodder and one instruction, so the only real trap is reading 'least surprisingly' together, as a comment on how obvious the answer ought to be.
explanation.definitionFit: The electric superstar -> TESLA: Nikola Tesla, the celebrated pioneer of alternating current, whose name now sits on a car as well.

clue.text: turning her into a fairy-tale vegetable, with temperature ready for baking (7)

indicators.note: a piece turned about ends up facing the other way, so its letters are read from the back
one word going into another lands inside it, splitting the host rather than sitting beside it

blocks.note: the princess in the tale felt one through twenty mattresses; the word opens after its first letter
the pronoun turned about, three letters read the other way
T is the standard abbreviation for temperature, on a dial or in a formula

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is a verb here — to ready something — and reading it as an adjective leaves the definition with nothing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: ready for baking -> PREHEAT: to preheat an oven is to bring it up to temperature before the food goes in, readying it.

clue.text: if wee kiss excited one of the parties after the marriage was over - (2-4)

definitions.text: one of the parties after the marriage was over

indicators.note: letters in an excited state will not stand still in the order they were handed to you

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, wee being the Scots word for small
X is the kiss written at the foot of a letter

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a wedding and the definition is what came long afterwards. Kiss = X is the step most solvers miss, and it is the letter the answer cannot do without.
explanation.definitionFit: one of the parties after the marriage was over -> EX-WIFE: the woman who was the wife, with ex- marking the relationship as ended.

clue.text: turned bawdy and there, not in our world, lived (5)

indicators.note: a word turned round is read from its far end back to its start
saying one thing is not in another is an instruction to take those letters out and keep what is left

blocks.note: LEWD means bawdy, and here it is read back to front
our world is HERE, and taking HERE out of THERE leaves one letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not in our world' sounds like a line about somewhere enchanted and is a subtraction: the other place with this one taken out of it.
explanation.definitionFit: lived -> DWELT: the past tense of dwell, to reside somewhere, and the form every fairy tale uses of where someone once lived.

clue.text: Little bird entered, empty inside, and ate (9)

indicators.note: a word emptied of its inside keeps nothing but the letters standing at its two ends

blocks.note: the small fork-tailed migrant that nests in barns
ENTERED hollowed out leaves its first and last letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'Little bird' sits at the front looking like a definition and is seven letters of the build; the definition is the three-letter word right at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: ate -> SWALLOWED: to swallow food is to get it down and so to have eaten it, a near synonym rather than an exact one.

clue.text: every bit, with difficulty (5)

blocks.note: w is the standard abbreviation for with, as in a recipe or a note
to be in a hole is to be in difficulty

explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like the joinery that holds a clue together and is a single letter. In a four-word clue there is no room for a word that is not working.
explanation.definitionFit: every bit -> WHOLE: the noun sense, as in 'the whole of it' — everything counted in, nothing left over.

clue.text: well, happily ever after (4)

indicators.note: the piece named as coming after the other is written second, which fixes the order of the two halves

blocks.note: being OK with something is being happy about it
ay is the old poetic word for ever, as in 'for ay'

explanation.walkthrough: The last clue of the puzzle is the last line of the story, so 'happily ever after' has to read as a set phrase and come apart into two pieces at the same time.
explanation.definitionFit: well -> OKAY: the adverb of health or progress — doing well, doing okay — rather than the deep hole in the ground.

clue.text: Critically out of depth, reluctantly (8)

indicators.note: taking one thing out of another removes it, and what is named here is a single letter of the longer word

blocks.note: an adverse review is a critical one, so this is the nine-letter word before the loss
d is the abbreviation for depth, and that is the letter coming out

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of depth' is a whole idiom in the surface — a critic beyond their expertise — and in the wordplay it is one letter leaving one word.
explanation.definitionFit: reluctantly -> AVERSELY: with aversion, doing a thing while disinclined to do it, the -ly answering the -ly.

clue.text: sounding like a stressed chicken (6)

indicators.note: what is wanted matches in speech and not in spelling, which is where the letters are free to change

blocks.note: a rope or a nerve under stress is frayed, and 'a frayed' said out loud is spelt quite differently

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chicken' reads as poultry in a clue full of fairy-tale animals, and the sense wanted is the playground one, a coward.
explanation.definitionFit: chicken -> AFRAID: the slang adjective for cowardly — calling somebody chicken says they have not the nerve for it.
